newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa defends arms sales to Rwanda.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa defends arms sales to Rwanda.

text.p: A top official overseeing South Africa's foreign weapons sales on Wednesday defended the country's controversial decision to sell arms to Rwanda's government.

South Africa was obliged to help the government in the central African state to establish order, Kader Asmal, the chairman of the statutory National Conventional Arms Control Committee (NCACC) appointed to vet arms exports, told a parliamentary committee.
"There has to be an element of acceptance of good faith, of good intentions...the (Rwandan) government is trying in a situation of virtual breakdown to assert some kind of jurisdiction," he said.
Asmal declined to say what was being sold to Rwanda, but gave an assurance that the deal did not include heavy weapons.

Tutsi-led rebels seized power in the central African country in July 1994 after fighting and genocidal massacres in which up to a million people were killed -- mainly Tutsis and moderate Hutus targeted for extermination.

The Hutu-dominated government that instigated the genocide was defeated in civil war and replaced by a new administration set up by the mainly Tutsi Rwanda Patriotic Front (RPF), whose forces had invaded from neighbouring Uganda in 1990.
Asmal said South Africa's former white government sold arms to factions responsible for the genocide, prior to 1994, without the sort of oversight provided by his committee.
The decision in late September to approve an unspecified arms deal with Rwanda has been criticised by South African opposition parties and the country's Anglican church.
Themba Khoza, of the mainly-Zulu based Inkatha Freedom Party, told Asmal the country had no business fuelling conflict in Rwanda.

"To me it is horrendous, it is awful. I am feeling my blood running cold that South Africa could sell arms to Rwanda. This is not a matter to run through and cover it up," he said in the parliamentary committee meeting.
Another Inkatha member, Albert Mncwango, said South Africa was arming one side in ethnic conflict that has also torn apart Burundi, Rwanda's southern neighbour.
